name: Body groomer (manscaping trimmer)

lead: A body groomer gives chest, abdomen and underarm hair a tidy, even length so the torso looks neater and more defined, without going fully bare. The change is visible immediately.

Guarded oscillating blades cut hair at a length set by an attachable guard, leaving short stubble rather than a skin-level cut. The technology descends from electric hair clippers, and no clinical research on the devices themselves was found.

paras: Men pick a guard length and run the trimmer over the chest, abdomen, underarms and other body areas, repeating as hair grows back. It is used as an alternative to shaving for a short, groomed look.
Risks are low. Clinical sources on ingrown hairs note that very close shaving can provoke them in people with curly hair, and that trimming to a short length is a common alternative.

chain: Hair looks tidy without bare skin
angle.text: A body groomer trims chest, abdomen and underarm hair to a tidy length so the torso looks neater and more defined without bare skin. The look is visible straight away; there is little research beyond general clipper literature.

lead: A body groomer, often sold as a manscaping trimmer, is an electric device with guarded blades for shortening or removing hair on the chest, abdomen, underarms and other areas below the neck.[1] People use it to keep body hair at a chosen short length, or to clear it entirely, so the physique looks cleaner and muscle definition reads more clearly.[2][3]

It descends from the electric hair clipper, which has been commercially available since the early 1920s, adapted into a smaller, rounded-blade format with attachable guards that set how much hair is left behind.[1] Trimming rather than razor-shaving is used by some people who find a short length a way to avoid the stubble and irritation that close shaving can bring.[4]

The practice has a long history. Wikipedia reports that body hair trimming goes back to ancient Egypt and Greece, where athletes did it, and that aesthetic body hair removal revived in recent decades, with the term manscaping first recorded in 2003.[3] No published studies specific to body groomers were identified.
infobox: Electric clipper, first patented 1921 (Leo J. Wahl)[1]

paras: Electric clippers are driven by a motor that oscillates the blades; motor designs include magnetic, rotary and pivot types, and attachable guards determine the length of hair left behind.[1] Body groomers apply this principle in a smaller, typically waterproof or rounded-blade format. Product details vary by manufacturer.

Manual clippers were reportedly invented around 1855 by the Serbian barber Nikola Bizumic, and Leo J. Wahl patented the first electric clipper in 1921, with Andis and Oster following in the same decade.[1] The dedicated body-hair variant is a later consumer product, and its marketing grew alongside the male grooming market, which Statista estimated at about US$81.2 billion globally by 2024.[3]

Wikipedia notes that bodybuilders and some athletes shave or reduce body hair to highlight muscle definition, and that some men also remove underarm hair.[2] Wikipedia's manscaping article adds that athletes in sports such as wrestling, swimming and cycling have trimmed hair for performance reasons.[3]

On T Nation, lifters mention light manscaping before progress photos, and one commenter wrote that a shave and tan is like an automatic ten-pound drop in how a physique looks.[5][6] These are anecdotal remarks.

No studies on body groomers were found. Wikipedia on pseudofolliculitis barbae describes ingrown hairs from close shaving in people with curly hair, and clinical advice for that condition often suggests leaving hair short but not skin-level, for example with a trimmer on a low setting.[4]

lore.intro: Body trimming comes up on T Nation threads as part of preparing for physique photos and gym culture; the threads are casual and anecdotal.[5][6]

claims.claim: Shaving or trimming body hair makes a physique look leaner.

timeline.event: Manual hair clippers reportedly invented by Nikola Bizumic.[1]
